VOXEU COLUMN
Adult social care can be better value than the health care we already fund
Joan Costa-i-Font  Sergi Jiménez-Martín  Cristina Vilaplana Prieto / 27 Oct 2026

Health programmes must clear cost-effectiveness thresholds, but social care faces no such test. This column uses Spain's 2007 long-term care reform to show that access to cash subsidies and publicly funded home help raised life satisfaction, reduced loneliness, and increased survival, at a cost per quality-adjusted life year well below the thresholds applied to health programmes. The results suggest that part of a national care service could be funded by replacing less cost-effective health programmes with social care.

AUTHORS
Joan Costa-i-Font
Sergi Jiménez-Martín
Cristina Vilaplana Prieto
SHARE
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Bluesky

Population ageing is raising the demand for long-term care. Across 30 developed countries, Kotschy and Bloom (2022) project that ageing will increase demand for care by 47% on average, ranging from 33% to 75% across countries, and report that 14.5% of those aged 65 and over, and 31.7% of those aged 80 and over, have two or more limitations in activities of daily living. Who will provide this care, and who will pay for it, is a pressing question (see also Kydland and Pretnar 2019).

Health programmes, by contrast, have to prove their worth. In England, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) applies a cost-effectiveness threshold of roughly £20,000–30,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. Social care faces no such test, so we know surprisingly little about what governments get, in health terms, for the money they spend helping older people with washing, dressing, cooking or getting about. The design of that spending matters. A previous VoxEU column (Barczyk and Kredler 2018) showed that generous long-term care policies crowd out family-provided care, and that informal care responds strongly even to small subsidies. This is why, in a recent paper (Costa-Font et al. 2026), we distinguish between cash subsidies and services.

A reform that changed who gets care

Spain offers a rare opportunity to find out what such spending achieves. Before 2007, publicly funded long-term care was scarce and means-tested, reserved for people with very high levels of need, and the unspoken expectation was that families, above all women, would cope. In January 2007, the System for Autonomy and Care for Dependent People (SAAD, created by Act 39/2006) established access based on assessed need, whatever a person's age. After an assessment, each person receives an individual care plan. This may include publicly funded home help, day centres, telecare or residential care, and it may also include a cash subsidy for families who provide care at home. The Spanish government agency IMSERSO publishes the benefit schedules and monthly statistics.

The rollout was gradual. In 2007, only people with the highest level of dependency were covered. Those with severe needs were added from around 2011, and moderate needs from 2015. Regions assess people and deliver services, so access also varied across Spain. Austerity then intervened. After Royal Decree 20/2012, caregiving subsidies were cut by 15%, co-payments rose, and hours of home help fell. This staggered, uneven expansion, followed by a retrenchment, gives us variation in who gets care and when.

What we did

We use the Spanish sample of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), a panel of people aged 50 and over, from 2004 to 2022. The main analysis excludes the 2020 pandemic wave, which was collected by telephone. We compare people who receive SAAD benefits with similar people who do not, before and after the reform. We match them on age, sex, marital status, education, income, and chronic conditions, and control for region and year effects. Our four outcomes are life satisfaction (0–10), loneliness (a 3–9 scale), depressive symptoms, and survival between survey waves.

SHARE has only two survey waves before the reform, so we complement the usual pre-trend checks with a sensitivity analysis that asks how large a violation of parallel trends would be needed to overturn the results (Rambachan and Roth 2023). Our estimates remain robust to violations up to twice the size of the largest pre-reform difference. Figure 1 shows how the four outcomes evolve around the reform.

Figure 1 Event study of the effect of access to long-term care services and supports on health and wellbeing

Notes: The panels show event-study coefficients for loneliness, life satisfaction, depressive symptoms (Euro-D > 3) and survival, for individuals receiving caregiving subsidies and home care supports. Period 0: implementation of SAAD. Period −1 corresponds to the pre-SAAD situation (2004). Periods 1 to 6 correspond to the situation after SAAD. 
Source: Own work using SHARE.
What we found

Access to care improves both wellbeing and survival. Among recipients of caregiving subsidies, life satisfaction rises by 0.24 points on the 0–10 scale. Among home help recipients it rises by 0.50, twice as much. Loneliness falls by about 0.6 points for subsidies and 0.5 for home help. The probability of surviving to the next survey wave rises by 3 percentage points for subsidies and 2.6 for home help. We also find fewer depressive symptoms.

The two types of support work slightly differently. Home help has the larger effect on life satisfaction, which is consistent with regular professional assistance and company. Subsidies have larger effects on survival and on loneliness and depression, perhaps because they allow families to arrange flexible care. The benefits are not evenly spread. They are larger for women, for people living alone and in rural areas, and for the oldest. Among people aged 80 and over, subsidies are associated with a 5.6 percentage point increase in survival.

What lies behind these gains? We cannot prove a single channel, but the pattern is consistent with the practical effects of care. Recipients report better diets, feel more in control of their lives and have fewer hip and other fractures, and their grip strength gap relative to non-recipients narrows after the reform. Regular help with daily tasks may plausibly prevent malnutrition, falls and the isolation that goes with unmet need.

The 2012–2017 austerity years are also informative. The cuts offset a substantial part of SAAD's benefits, with loneliness and depression rising and life satisfaction and survival falling relative to the counterfactual. Retrenching care is not free: the costs show up in health and well-being.

Is it good value for money?

Our second question is whether these gains justify the cost. This is the question health systems routinely ask of drugs and treatments, but rarely of social care. To answer it, we combine our estimates with data on what each type of benefit costs recipients' public funders and relate the cost to the quality-adjusted life years gained. This is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a full economic evaluation, but it gives an order of magnitude, reported in Figure 2.

We estimate that caregiving subsidies cost around €6,200 per QALY gained and home help around €9,200. Cost-effectiveness thresholds across Europe typically range from €20,000 to €50,000 per QALY, and NICE's range is higher than our estimates. Even for the least cost-effective groups we identify, such as women aged 55–59 receiving home help, the estimate is about €17,500 per QALY. That is still below the usual thresholds. In other words, on these estimates, the average euro spent on long-term care buys health gains at a price that compares favourably with the health programmes that systems already fund.

Figure 2 Cost per QALY (euros per year)

Notes: Purple bars represent the cost per QALY for men receiving caregiving subsidies; green bars for women receiving caregiving subsidies; red bars for men receiving home care supports; and yellow bars for women receiving home care supports. Vertical lines indicate 95% confidence intervals. The cost per QALY is calculated based on life expectancy by sex and age cohort. 
Source: Own calculations using SHARE data.
What this means 

These findings matter beyond Spain. In the UK, as in Spain, the system relies heavily on unpaid family carers, and NHS and social care budgets are set and judged separately. Health programmes must clear a cost-effectiveness bar, while social care is largely exempt. Yet the NHS is under constant pressure to ration, and NICE's threshold is itself a statement that some spending on health care is not worth its cost. Claxton et al. (2015) estimate the NHS's marginal cost per QALY, the productivity of the last pound spent, at around £13,000 (2008 prices), lower than the NICE threshold. Our estimates for the average recipient of long-term care are of the same order or lower, although currencies and price years differ and subgroups vary.

This suggests that, in the UK, part of a social care service could be financed by replacing NHS programmes that fall short of the cost-effectiveness bar with social care programmes, such as home help, that deliver more health per pound. Moving resources across the NHS and social care boundary is hard, and our results do not tell us how such restructuring should happen. What they do indicate is that the health returns to home help and carer support are real, show up in survival and well-being, and can be at least as large per pound as the returns to many things the NHS buys. A social care service that is evaluated on the same terms as health care, and funded in part by reallocating from less cost-effective health programmes, would be a better use of limited resources than the status quo.

For policymakers, the implication is that long-term care should be routinely assessed with the same health-economic tools as medical interventions, including measures of loneliness, depression and life satisfaction. And where budgets are tight, the right question is not whether to fund health or social care, but which spending, wherever it sits, buys the most health.

References

Barczyk, D and M Lredler (2018), “Long-term care across the Atlantic: How policy shapes care arrangements”, VoxEU.org, 28 January. 

Claxton, K, S Martin, M Soares et al. (2015), “Methods for the estimation of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence cost-effectiveness threshold”, Health Technology Assessment 19(14).

Costa-Font, J, S Jiménez-Martín and C Vilaplana-Prieto (2026), “Returns to caring? Health and well-being effects of subsidized long-term care”, Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, e70136.

Kotschy, R and D E Bloom (2022), “Reckoning with the growing demand for long-term care”, VoxEU.org, 25 May (see also IZA Discussion Paper 15228).

Kydland, F and N Pretnar (2019), “Who will care for all the old people?”, in Live Long and Prosper? The Economics of Ageing Populations, CEPR Press.

Rambachan, A and J Roth (2023), “A more credible approach to parallel trends”, Review of Economic Studies 90(5): 2555–2591.

AUTHORS
Joan Costa-i-Font

Professor of Health Economics London School Of Economics And Political Science

Sergi Jiménez-Martín

Director, LaCaixa-FEDEA chair on Health Economics Foundation for Applied Economic Studies (FEDEA); Professor of Economics Pompeu Fabra University

Cristina Vilaplana Prieto

Professor University of Murcia

VOXEU COLUMN COMPETITION POLICY
How agreements between suppliers and retailers can weaken competition
Zhonglin Li  Hsin-Tien Tiffany Tsai / 27 Oct 2026

Agreements between manufacturers and retailers can affect competition across brands and stores. This column documents retail price patterns in the US consumer battery industry and uses a model estimated from purchase data to explore two potential mechanisms: changes in downstream retail pricing and changes in upstream wholesale contracting. Counterfactual simulations illustrate how these mechanisms could jointly weaken competition. In the scenarios examined, the wholesale channel generates the larger consumer welfare loss. The findings highlight the importance of considering both channels when evaluating the potential effects of vertical agreements.

SHARE
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Bluesky
AUTHORS
Zhonglin Li

Assistant Professor National University Of Singapore

Hsin-Tien Tiffany Tsai

Associate Professor National University Of Singapore

Recent litigation involving the retailer Walmart and the battery manufacturer Energizer raises a broader policy question about agreements between suppliers and retailers. The plaintiffs allege that the companies sought to raise the wholesale prices charged to Walmart's rivals and prevent other retailers from undercutting Walmart's retail prices (US District Court for the Northern District of California 2026). These allegations raise a broader economic question: how might competition be affected by vertical arrangements that influence both retail pricing incentives and the wholesale costs faced by competing retailers?

A manufacturer supplies products to several competing stores, while each store carries products from competing manufacturers. These relationships mean that changes in one firm's pricing incentives or wholesale terms can have effects beyond the firms directly involved. Assessing the potential consequences of vertical restraints requires considering how the market would operate under alternative arrangements, including the responses of competing manufacturers and retailers.

Earlier research helps explain why these interactions matter. Salop and Scheffman (1983) showed how firms can profit by raising rivals' costs. Luco and Marshall (2020), studying soft drinks, found that vertical integration could lower prices for some products while raising prices for others sold by the integrated firm. Herweg and Müller (2015) explain how the effects of wholesale price discrimination depend on contract structures and the information available to firms. These studies highlight how vertical relationships can affect pricing incentives and competition across products and retailers.

Two connected routes to higher prices

To make the mechanisms concrete, consider two battery brands – Energizer and its competitor Duracell – sold by Walmart and competing retailers. Suppose Walmart and Energizer take each other's profits into account when setting prices. Walmart would then have an incentive to raise Duracell's price and steer customers towards Energizer. Competition between brands could weaken even though both remain on the shelf.

The same arrangement could also affect wholesale pricing. Energizer may have less incentive to offer attractive wholesale terms to retailers that compete with Walmart. Higher wholesale prices could lead to higher retail prices at those stores, reducing the competitive pressure on Walmart. The two mechanisms therefore affect different dimensions of competition: one changes pricing incentives within Walmart, while the other raises costs for competing retailers.

Together, these mechanisms connect competition between brands with competition between retailers. Related research also highlights how wholesale contracts can influence competition between distribution channels (Jullien et al. 2022).

Price patterns across brands and retailers

In a recent paper (Li and Tsai 2026), we use household purchase receipts from the US consumer battery industry. The data record which products consumers buy, where they buy them, and what they pay. We first use these data to document retail price patterns across brands and retailers.

Figures 1a and 1b show quarterly retail price indices for Energizer and Duracell at Walmart and competing retailers, with each series normalised to one in 2019Q1. An index of 1.10 indicates that the price index is 10% higher than its 2019Q1 level. These indices capture changes over time within each series rather than differences in actual price levels across brands or retailers.

Figure 1 Retail price changes by brand at Walmart and other retailers

a) Walmart

b) Other retailers

Notes: Each series in Figures 1a and 1b is normalised to one in 2019Q1. The vertical dashed line marks 2019Q2. Figure 1b includes Dollar Tree as a comparison series. The indices show changes relative to each series' baseline, rather than differences in actual price levels. 
Source: Authors' calculations.

At Walmart, Duracell's price rises sharply in 2019Q2 and subsequently remains above its baseline (Figure 1a). Energizer's price also rises, but by less. By 2021Q3, Duracell's price is approximately 8.5% above its 2019Q1 level, compared with about 6% for Energizer. Duracell's larger price increase could make Energizer relatively more attractive at Walmart, even though both brands become more expensive.

Outside Walmart, the pattern differs (Figure 1b). Both brands' prices increase after 2019Q1, but from 2020 onwards, Energizer's increase is consistently larger than Duracell's. By 2021Q3, Energizer's price is approximately 15% above its baseline, compared with about 8.5% for Duracell. The Dollar Tree comparison series remains flat over the same period.

Figure 2 shows that price changes also vary considerably across retailers. Dollar General records the largest sustained increase, with its index approximately 25% above the baseline by 2021Q3. Prices also rise at Walmart, Costco, Target, and the retailers grouped as “Others”, although by different amounts. Amazon shows no sustained increase, while Dollar Tree's index remains at one.

Figure 2 Retail price changes across retailers

Notes: Each retailer's price index is normalised to one in 2019Q1. The vertical dashed line marks 2019Q2. The indices show changes relative to each retailer's baseline, rather than differences in actual price levels. 
Source: Authors' calculations.

These patterns are consistent with the two potential mechanisms described above. At Walmart, a larger increase in Duracell's price could steer purchases towards Energizer. At competing retailers, less favourable wholesale terms for Energizer could lead to larger increases in its retail price. Together, these mechanisms illustrate how vertical agreements could affect both competition between brands within a store and competition between stores selling the same brand.

The price patterns alone do not establish whether the alleged agreement took place or caused the observed changes, nor do they identify the contribution of each mechanism. They motivate our model, which allows us to examine the two channels separately and quantify their potential consequences for consumers.

Quantifying the two channels

To examine the potential consumer welfare implications of the two mechanisms, we use household purchase data to estimate demand and infer costs, providing the basis for simulations of competition between manufacturers and retailers (Li and Tsai 2026). The simulations allow consumers to switch between brands and retailers while holding total battery purchases fixed.

We estimate the model using data from before the alleged conduct, which we call the pre-period. The benchmark assumes that the hypothesised agreement is absent. Manufacturers bargain with retailers over wholesale terms, and retailers choose prices across the brands they carry. Firms can have market power in this benchmark, but each maximises its own profits. Consumer substitution between brands and stores determines how strongly the firms constrain one another.

Starting from this benchmark, we use retail prices observed after the alleged conduct began, together with the corresponding wholesale prices inferred in Li and Tsai (2026), to estimate brand- and retailer-specific price changes and apply them to the pre-period market. This constructs a hypothetical agreement scenario under the assumption that the post-period price changes reflect the hypothesised agreement. The exercise therefore asks what the welfare consequences would be under this interpretation, rather than establishing that the agreement caused the observed price changes.

To examine the two channels separately, we hold either Walmart's Duracell retail prices or Energizer's wholesale prices charged to competing retailers at their scenario levels, allowing the remaining prices and wholesale terms to adjust in the model.

In these simulations, both mechanisms generate consumer welfare losses. The wholesale channel generates approximately 2.2 to 3.4 times the consumer welfare loss of the retail channel across the specifications considered. Combining both mechanisms generates larger losses than either alone.

Implications for competition enforcement

First, different types of vertical restraints may be implemented together and interact with one another. Retail pricing incentives and wholesale terms can jointly influence competition across brands and retailers. Our simulations suggest that considering these mechanisms in isolation may overlook their combined effects on consumers.

Second, wholesale restraints may have important consequences beyond the firms directly involved. By raising the costs of competing retailers, changes in wholesale terms can affect retail prices throughout the market. In our simulations, the wholesale channel generates larger consumer welfare losses than the retail channel. This highlights the importance of looking beyond observed retail prices when assessing potential competitive effects (see also Gado et al. 2024).

Third, the effects on competing firms can be less straightforward. Our simulations suggest that Walmart and Energizer earn higher joint profits, while competing retailers' profits fall in aggregate. Duracell may also benefit through improved wholesale terms with other retailers, despite losing sales at Walmart. This illustrates that even firms not directly involved in an arrangement may benefit from weaker competition, while consumers are worse off.

These considerations also matter for remedies. If potential harm arises through both retail and wholesale mechanisms, addressing only one may leave the other operating. Evaluating remedies requires accounting for how firms would adjust their prices and contracts, as well as possible efficiencies generated by vertical arrangements. 

Editors’ note: This column is published in collaboration with the International Economic Associations’ Women in Leadership in Economics initiative, which aims to enhance the role of women in economics through research, building partnerships, and amplifying voices.

References

Gado, K, R Schoenle and S Thomas (2024), “The role of shipping costs in platform retail competition”, VoxEU.org, 9 November. 

Herweg, F and D Müller (2015), “Price discrimination by big manufacturers: Supporting arguments for its prohibition by European competition law”, VoxEU.org, 7 April. 

Jullien, B, M Reisinger and P Rey (2022), “Personalised pricing and distribution strategies”, VoxEU.org, 25 August.

Li, Z and H-T Tsai (2026), “Vertical Control and Retail Competition: Evidence from Consumer Battery Industry”, working paper, National University of Singapore. 

Luco, F and G Marshall (2020), “The competitive impact of vertical inte

VOXEU COLUMN FINANCIAL MARKETS INDUSTRIAL ORGANISATION
Private equity beyond the target: How buyouts reshape supply chains
Olivier De Jonghe  Cédric Huylebroek / 26 Oct 2026

The importance of private equity for euro area firms is increasing, with annual growth rates in assets under management exceeding 10%. Private equity buyouts affect more than just the firms being acquired. Using comprehensive data for Belgium, this column shows that the sales volumes of suppliers grow faster when there is a higher proportion of business with customers backed by private equity. But this advantage is lost during downturns, as investors push for cost savings. Buyouts can also crowd out competitors that depend on the same suppliers. Finally, high leverage implies greater interest rate sensitivity, so private equity buyouts can intensify the transmission of monetary policy to target firms and beyond.

SHARE
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Bluesky
AUTHORS
Olivier De Jonghe

Lead Economist European Central Bank; Senior Economist National Bank Of Belgium

Cédric Huylebroek

Economist Deutsche Bundesbank; Economist at the Deutsche Bundesbank Katholieke Universiteit Leuven

Private equity (PE) buyouts are often judged by what happens inside the acquired company: does it grow or become more productive, does its management improve? Past research has documented the effects on jobs and productivity of firms being bought out by private equity (Davis et al. 2014). In line with their results, in a recent paper (Huylebroek and De Jonghe 2026) we find that after a PE buyout the financial leverage of target firms significantly increases and they grow faster than their peers (or ‘matched controls’). Moreover, also consistent with previous studies, we find that target firms outperform their peers even more strongly during economic downturns, when PE investors’ managerial expertise may be particularly valuable (Bernstein et al. 2019). 

However, firms do not operate in isolation. They buy inputs from suppliers, sell to customers and compete with other firms that may rely on the same production networks. A change in ownership can therefore affect businesses well beyond the company that is being acquired.

We examine these effects using data from Belgium. The dataset links firm-to-firm sales, company accounts and PE transactions for 2002-21. It covers virtually all firms, including small private companies, which are the targets of most PE buyouts but are often absent from commercial supply-chain data. 

We compare the economic trajectories, both before and after a buyout, of two types of firms: suppliers linked to customers backed by PE, and similar suppliers connected to customers not backed by PE.

Figure 1 How to examine the effect of buyouts on suppliers of target firms?

Notes: This figure illustrates our empirical strategy for estimating how PE buyouts affect target firms’ suppliers. Suppose one of Supplier A’s customers is acquired by a PE firm in year t. Our difference-in-differences design compares Supplier A’s economic trajectory before and after the acquisition with that of a comparable Supplier B without a PE-backed customer.
Growing customers boost suppliers

After a PE buyout, suppliers of the acquired firm perform better than comparable suppliers not linked to a PE-backed customer. Across the full post-buyout period their sales are around 8% higher and employment around 4% higher (Figure 2). 

Figure 2 Sales and employment growth of suppliers of the acquired firm

Dynamic difference-in-differences estimates for the effect of PE buyouts on suppliers of target firms

Source: Huylebroek and De Jonghe (2026).
Notes: This chart presents the dynamic difference-in-differences estimates of the effect of PE buyouts on the suppliers of target firms. The y-axis corresponds to the coefficient estimates (dots). The vertical bars represent confidence intervals at the 95% level. The x-axis corresponds to years relative to the year in which the target firm was acquired. The outcome variables are, in the left-hand panel, the natural logarithm of sales and, in the right-hand panel, the natural logarithm of employees.

The evidence points to an explanation: PE-backed firms pursue new growth opportunities and increase their purchases of inputs. 

The suppliers already embedded in their production process receive more orders and respond by expanding. The gains are strongest when either the target has more room to grow, the supplier provides a relatively large share of the target’s inputs, or the relationship between them is more established.

Customer-level comparisons confirm that the increase in supplier sales is driven mainly by purchases from PE-backed customers. 

Demand matters more than knowledge transfer

A buyout can benefit suppliers through knowledge transfer, trade credit and/or certification as result of the change of ownership. 

We establish that suppliers do not increase research and development or highly skilled employment and changes in trade credit are not significant. Some suppliers gain customers within the PE investor’s network, but this reputational ‘certification effect’ is small compared with the direct increase in demand.

Downturns reverse the balance

The pattern changes sharply when the economy weakens.

During downturns, suppliers of PE-backed firms no longer outperform their peers. Their markups fall by approximately 8%, suggesting that they concede part of the value created in the buyer-supplier relationship through lower prices or less favourable terms.

We attribute this reversal to more intensive PE involvement in cost-cutting. This is consistent with evidence that PE investors can be especially active when portfolio companies face financial fragility (Bernstein et al. 2019). Buyouts are typically leveraged, so preserving cash and meeting debt obligations become particularly important when sales and profits come under pressure. Investors can seek savings by renegotiating contracts, threatening to switch suppliers or actively redesigning the supply chain.

The pressure is concentrated on suppliers with weaker bargaining positions. It is greater for suppliers of standardised inputs, which are easier to replace, and for suppliers operating in highly competitive industries where customers have more alternatives. The pressure is also greater when the PE investor is larger and more experienced, as measured by past deal activity.

Consistent with this interpretation, PE-backed firms are more likely to terminate supplier relationships during downturns as they reduce their input costs.

Shared suppliers can transmit the shock to rivals

The market structure consequences of PE buyouts extend beyond direct suppliers. A PE-backed firm that expands may absorb more of a supplier’s available capacity. Its competitors, especially those relying on the same upstream firms, may then find it harder to maintain their relationships if suppliers prioritise their faster growing PE-backed customers over others, as illustrated in Figure 3.

Figure 3 Crowding-out competitors

Illustration of potential crowding-out effects of PE-backed firms on other firms through shared suppliers

We find that suppliers affected by a PE buyout are more likely to terminate relationships with rivals of their PE-backed customers. 

This finding connects to research showing how shared suppliers and bargaining relationships can shape downstream competition (Giannetti et al. 2021). The pattern is strongest when supplier capacity is constrained and when their rivals are already performing poorly, which is consistent with suppliers prioritising fast-growing customers.

The effect is economically meaningful. An increase of one standard deviation in a competitor’s exposure to common suppliers is associated with a 1% decline in employment, a 2% decline in core earnings (EBITDA) and a 1% decline in markups. More broadly, the result illustrates how firm-level shocks can propagate through production networks (Acemoglu et al. 2012), even when the acquired firm and its rivals do not have a direct ownership link.

Implications for policy

Overall, our findings underscore the central role of supply chains in understanding how PE investors create and redistribute value. 

On average, PE ownership benefits upstream suppliers, but PE-owned firms exert greater pressure on suppliers during periods of economic distress. These results suggest that policymakers, such as central banks and competition authorities, as well as practitioners should consider the full implications of changing ownership patterns. These encompass not only the direct effects of PE investments but also the broader spillover effects on supply chains and the implications for market competition. In some countries, listed firms are required to publicly disclose their primary suppliers. Regulators could utilise this information to assess the degree of upstream overlap between PE targets and their competitors before approving a transaction.

Our finding that PE buyouts benefit suppliers through increased input demand – an effect we do not observe for firms funded by bank debt – can inform the debate on the role of bank versus non-bank financing in stimulating economic growth.

Finally, and more broadly, our findings suggest that the growing role of PE may ramp up the transmission of monetary policy through production networks. PE activity and financing conditions are particularly sensitive to the interest rate environment (Ivashina 2022). Therefore, tighter monetary policy could affect suppliers more by inducing highly leveraged PE-backed firms to shift away from expanding, which benefits them, towards stronger cost cutting, supplier bargaining, and supply-chain reconfiguration.

Authors’ note: This column first appeared as a Research Bulletin of the European Central Bank. The authors gratefully acknowledge the comments from Diana Bonfim, Jonathan Drake and Alexander Popov.
